issue.issue_text: Whether the imputation made by the appellant is protected by the First Exception to Section 499 of the Indian Penal Code, which requires the imputation to be true and made for the public good.

facts: The appellant, the President of a Municipal Committee, made defamatory remarks about a nurse.
The appellant claimed his statements were justified under several exceptions to Section 499 of the Indian Penal Code, including the First Exception.
law: The First Exception to Section 499 of the Indian Penal Code protects an imputation from being defamatory if two conditions are met: 1) the imputation must be true, and 2) it must be made for the public good.
The burden of proving both of these conditions rests on the person who made the imputation (the appellant).
application: The Supreme Court found that the appellant "totally failed to establish" that his statements met the requirements of the First Exception.
The Court determined that the evidence showed the imputation against the nurse was not true.
Furthermore, the Court concluded that the appellant's statements were not made for the public good but were instead "motivated by animus" (personal ill will) against the nurse.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's defense under the First Exception because he failed to prove that his defamatory statements were true and that they were made for the public good.

issue.issue_text: Whether the communication made by the appellant was protected by the defense of privilege.

facts: The appellant, who was the President of a local Municipal Committee, wrote a letter to the Civil Surgeon containing defamatory statements about the complainant, a nurse.
The appellant was convicted of defamation under Section 500 of the Indian Penal Code.
On appeal, the appellant argued that the letter sent to the Civil Surgeon was a privileged communication.
law: The defense of privilege extends only to a communication made on the specific subject for which the privilege exists.
The privilege can only be claimed when it is exercised to safeguard the right or interest that is the source of the privilege.
application: The Court first noted that the specific plea—that the appellant had a duty as Municipal President to write to the Civil Surgeon about the complainant's work—was never raised during the trial.
Furthermore, the Court found there was no evidence presented to support this claim of duty.
The Court examined the 'concurrent findings of fact' from the lower courts, which it found 'repel any suggestion' that the appellant wrote the letter to protect a legitimate interest.
The appellant failed to provide any material to show how the defamatory 'insinuations' in the letter were made in protection of his interest.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the defense of privilege because the plea was not made at trial, there was no evidence to support it, and the communication went beyond the scope of any interest the appellant might have been trying to protect.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The onus of proving that a defamatory imputation is true and that its publication is for the public good rests on the person making the imputation.
obiter: A person of power and wealth should act with restraint and decorum.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The appellant, a man of power and wealth and the President of the Municipal Committee, failed to act with the restraint, decorum, prudence, and caution required of his position. The court found that his defamatory imputations against the respondent were not made in good faith or for the public good, but were motivated by animus. Consequently, the appellant completely failed to establish the necessary ingredients to claim protection under any of the exceptions to Section 499 of the Indian Penal Code.
legal_tests_applied: First Exception to Section 499 IPC: To claim this exception, the accused must prove two ingredients: (1) that the imputation is true, and (2) that the publication of the imputation is for the public good. The onus of proving both is on the accused.

Test for Good Faith: 'In order to establish good faith and bona fide it has to be seen first the circumstance under which the letter was written or words were uttered: secondly. whether there was any malice: thirdly, whether the appellant made any enquiry before he made the allegations; fourthly. whether there are reasons to accept the version that he acted with care and caution and finally whether there is preponderance of probability that the appellant acted in good faith.'

Ninth Exception to Section 499 IPC: An imputation is not defamation if it is 'made in good faith for the protection of the interest of the person making it, or of !lny other person, or for the pubhc good.' The interest of the person 'has to be real and legitimate when communication is made in protection of the interest of the person making it.'

Test for Privilege: 'The privilege extends only to a communication upon the subject with respect to which the privilege extends and the privilege can be claimed in exercise of the right or safeguard of the interest which creates the privilege.'
why_appellant_lost: The appellant totally failed to establish the two ingredients of the First Exception, as the onus was on him to prove both the truth of the imputation and that its publication was for the public good.
The evidence indicated that the imputation concerning the respondent was not true and was, on the contrary, 'motivated by animus of the appellant against the respondent.'
The appellant's plea of good faith was rejected, with the court noting 'facts which dispel any semblance of good faith and indicate on the contrary lack of prudence and dignity.'
The appellant's argument that he acted pursuant to a resolution from residents was found to have 'no foundation' in light of the findings of fact.
Regarding the claim of privilege, the court noted that 'This plea was not taken and there is no evidence to support it.'
The appellant failed to show that the communication was made in protection of any of his real and legitimate interests, as required to claim privilege or the Ninth Exception.
why_respondent_won: The respondent won because the appellant failed to discharge the onus of proving that his defamatory statements fell under any of the statutory exceptions.
The court accepted the evidence that the imputation was not true, but was instead motivated by the appellant's animus towards the respondent.
The concurrent findings of fact from the lower courts repelled any suggestion that the appellant acted in good faith or to protect a legitimate interest.
policy_considerations: A person's position regulates the standard of care and caution required of them: 'The position of the person making the imputation will regulate the standard -Of care and caution.'

Individuals in positions of power and authority are held to a higher standard of conduct. 'The appellant was a man.of power and wealth. That is all the more why he should have acted with restraint and decorum. He failed in both.'
Public officials, like the President of a Municipal Committee, are 'required to act .with utmost orudence and caution.'
